groups.text: A card issuer's reply arrives as one class: a status, and four optional fields.
Count the shapes it allows.
Three statuses, and four fields that are each set or null.
That's forty-eight shapes.
How many of them make sense?
Three. The other forty-five can still be built and passed around, like approved with no auth code.
Every consumer has to re-check, and one won't: the capture job sends null as the auth code.
Model the three outcomes instead, each with only its own fields: a sealed AuthResult with three records.
Now there are three shapes.
Approved with a decline code can't even be written down.
The checks that are left move into the constructors: an auth code is six letters or digits, and an approved amount is positive.
That's what make illegal states unrepresentable means.
The model only helps if raw data can't get in around it.
So the service parses input into the model in one place, at its edge.
parse never throws.
A good reply comes out as a model value.
One the model refuses comes back as Rejected, with a reason.
Behind the edge, nothing re-validates.
A method that takes an Approved knows its code is valid, because no other kind of Approved can exist.
And the logic?
The records stay plain.
Each operation is one function with a switch over the three kinds.
Brian Goetz calls this style data-oriented programming.
A new operation is a new function that touches nothing else.
The price: a new kind breaks every switch, and the compiler lists them.
In Java, that's a sealed interface and three records.
In Kotlin, a sealed interface and three data classes.
And one parse function at the edge.
The rule: make bad combinations impossible to build.
Parse raw input into them once, at the edge.
And keep the logic in functions over the data.
Quick check. Behind the edge, a method takes an Approved.
Does it need to check the auth code for null?
No. Every Approved went through its constructor, so no other kind of Approved can exist.
